source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Founding paper. Epistemic actions are physical actions that make mental computation easier, faster or more reliable. Tetris was chosen because every move either brings a piece closer to its final place or not, so pragmatic and non-pragmatic moves are easy to tell apart.
numbers: Data: keystroke logs, tachistoscopic mental-rotation tests, an expert-system player (RoboTetris). Board 10x30; fall speed 200 to 100 ms per square.
limits: Epistemic = external, physical action; authors admit one action can be both epistemic and pragmatic at once.
agent_relevance: Gives the definition we need for S4: a probe is an action whose value is the information it returns, not progress.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) rotation counts vs plan-first model
finding: If players planned first and then acted, rotations per piece would average half the possible rotations (1.5 for a four-orientation piece). Observed rotations exceeded this for every piece type, and rotation began by 400 to 600 ms.
numbers: Fig 6 and 7: average rotations above the expected pragmatic number for each zoid, 95% CI shown; exact per-zoid values not readable in text extraction.
limits: Evidence is indirect: extra rotations could also be false starts. The authors argue false starts do not fit the timing (75 ms between keystrokes in a burst, about 250 ms on average).
agent_relevance: Agents that plan fully, then act, miss cheap early probes; the data favour interleaving.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) physical vs mental rotation speed
finding: A physical 90 degree rotation takes as little as 100 ms. Mental rotation of a zoid 90 degrees is estimated at 800 to 1200 ms. Physical rotation also avoids memory and attention costs of holding an image.
numbers: Pilot mental rotation task, 3 Tetris players (intermediate, advanced, expert), 8 presentations of each pair; reaction time rose linearly with angle difference 0 to 180 degrees. Authors allow an extra 200 ms for choosing the rotate key.
limits: Pilot with N=3 and no statistics reported. The mental rotation estimate is an extrapolation, not measured on a piece in play.
agent_relevance: Cost ratio is the core: probe cost 100 to 300 ms against 800 to 1200 ms of internal simulation. For an LLM the analogue is a cheap code run against a long chain of thought.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) early rotation to expose hidden shape
finding: A new zoid is partly hidden as it enters. Rotating it reveals the whole shape 150 to 300 ms earlier than waiting for it to fall into view.
numbers: Zoid falls one square per 150 ms at medium speed, so the full image takes about 0.5 s. Authors predicted good players would find this strategy and say they do.
limits: Prediction plus observation; no controlled test of whether players who rotate early are faster or more accurate.
agent_relevance: Closest match to 'act to reveal hidden information': a probe that returns a missing observation.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) translate-to-wall verification
finding: In about 1% of drops, players move the zoid to the wall and back to check its column before dropping. They do this more when the drop is higher, because the column judgment is less reliable.
numbers: Table 1 mean drop distance (squares): ordinary 13.18 intermediate, 13.69 advanced, 15.65 expert; after the verify routine 19.04, 19.33, 20.05. Each skill level differs at alpha .05. Fig 15: probability rises with drop height.
limits: Only about 1% of drops. Chosen as the unambiguous case because it cannot be a pragmatic move. Effect size not reported beyond t-test significance.
agent_relevance: A clean example of verification as cost-benefit: probe more when the risk of error is higher. Rule: probe in proportion to the cost of a wrong attempt.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) cost-benefit model of when to act epistemically
finding: Epistemic value of an action depends on time: a rotation made late has less value because the information would have arrived anyway. At great height the cost of moving away from the goal is outweighed by the error reduction.
numbers: Qualitative cost-benefit sketch; no fitted parameters.
limits: No quantitative model fitted in the paper; Maglio, Wenger and Copeland 2003 test it.
agent_relevance: Supports a stopping rule for probing: stop when expected information gain falls below action cost.

source: Maglio & Wenger (2000) Two views are better than one: epistemic actions may prime
finding: A preview of a Tetris shape (a second view) made fit judgments faster and more accurate. A second view in a different orientation primed as well as one in the same orientation. A third view added nothing.
numbers: N=30 recruited, 3 days of one hour, 480 trials per session. One preview vs none: accuracy 0.86 vs 0.53, t(59)=33.85; RT 869 ms vs 1791 ms, t(59)=2.01, p<.05. Number of previews (1 vs 2), retention interval, and preview orientation had no effect on RT or accuracy (all F<1).
limits: Abstract task with 250 ms displays, not real play. Direct vs indirect memory test differed only on day-1 latency. The RT test is weak (p just under .05). Priming, not mental-rotation substitution, is what the data support.
agent_relevance: The benefit comes from a cue that reactivates memory, not from replacing a computation. Probes may help by priming recall, a different mechanism from 'running the test'.

source: Maglio, Wenger & Copeland (2003) The benefits of epistemic action outweigh the costs
finding: Using hazard-function analysis of reaction times, previews raised processing capacity by about 38%. The benefit exceeded the time cost of the extra rotation plus correction at every lag, and the ratio grew as lag grew.
numbers: N=15 (Notre Dame). Mean RT with preview 528 ms vs 673 ms without, t=5.09, p<.0001. Hazard model: prime presence chi2=96.85, change 37.8%. Benefit-to-cost ratio rises with lag, F(2,28)=31.25. Cost = 2x keypress RT added to a 4.4 s fixed trial time.
limits: Cost overestimates expert cost (authors note). Pieces shown 250 ms each in a restricted version of Tetris; capacity is inferred, not observed in real play. Small N; one lab.
agent_relevance: First quantitative test that epistemic action pays. Benefit is largest when memory load is highest, so probe most when the reasoning chain is long.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill
finding: Reported (as described by later papers) that experts take more actions and more backtracking than novices in Tetris.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Not opened. Described in Maglio et al. 2003 and in Destefano and Gray 2007 only.
agent_relevance: The claim that probing grows with expertise is contested; see Destefano and Gray 2007.

source: Destefano & Gray (2007) Use of complimentary actions decreases with expertise
finding: Failed replication of the expertise claim. In a tournament sample, the frequency of complementary actions fell as skill rose, in direct contradiction to Maglio and Kirsh 1996. Authors suspect many extra moves are goal switching after a motor plan was already started.
numbers: Players sorted into four levels (novice, intermediate, advanced, expert) by the better of two game scores; data binned by fall speed. Sample size and effect sizes are not given in the 2-page poster.
limits: Two-page poster; no N, no statistics. Coding 'complementary' vs error is the hard part; eye-tracking was planned but not done. Convention-attendee sample.
agent_relevance: Extra actions are not automatically epistemic. Log probes separately from plan changes before crediting probing.

source: Destefano & Gray (2007) method: comparing skill at matched speed
finding: Novices and experts were compared only at the same falling-block speed so skill was not confounded with speed. Time to place a block, time between actions and first-move latency all fell with expertise.
numbers: Millisecond logging; four skill levels; N not stated.
limits: Cannot tell whether the earlier increase with skill came from pooling across speeds.
agent_relevance: Measurement lesson: compare probe rate at matched difficulty, not pooled.

source: Kaye (2013) Tetris and mental rotation (M.A. thesis, UKZN)
finding: Banning physical rotation in Tetris did not reduce the mental-rotation training benefit. Neither Tetris group beat the non-Tetris control. So epistemic rotation does not seem to matter for transfer.
numbers: N=13 Tetris with physical rotation disabled, N=13 standard Tetris, N=14 control. Five one-hour lab sessions over five weeks; mental rotation tested before and after.
limits: Small groups. Tests transfer, not in-game performance; Tetris did not beat control, so the base effect was not reproduced. Read from the repository abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: epistemic action's payoff is local to the task, not a general skill gain.

source: Neth & Muller (2008) Thinking by doing and doing by thinking: a taxonomy of actions
finding: Argues the epistemic/pragmatic split is confusing: pragmatic actions can seem epistemic and the reverse. Proposes goal-relative classes, focal vs ancillary, and theoretical (mental-state) vs practical (world) actions. Physical actions that replace mental ones become practical ancillary actions chosen as a contingent alternative.
numbers: Conceptual paper; no experiment.
limits: Terminology paper, not data. The word 'epistemic' in philosophy or AI means something different from Kirsh and Maglio's sense.
agent_relevance: Define each probe relative to a stated goal and treat it as a cheaper substitute for thought.

source: Maglio, Wenger & Copeland (2003) summary of Neth & Payne 2002, Gray & Fu 2000, Kirlik 1998
finding: States that Neth and Payne found epistemic actions benefit steady-state behaviour but help during learning in the Tower of Hanoi. Gray and Fu found people trade time and accuracy depending on task layout. Kirlik tested a formal version on short-order cooks.
numbers: Secondhand summary only; no numbers.
limits: Secondhand description inside the 2003 paper; originals were not opened.
agent_relevance: Costs of acting must be weighed against information gained; not all actions are worth taking.

source: Neth & Payne (2002) Thinking by doing? Epistemic actions in the Tower of Hanoi
finding: Tower of Hanoi study cited as showing extra actions help. Original paper not opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only the 2003 description was read.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a deeper read.

source: Gray & Fu (2000) Influence of source and cost of information access
finding: People shift between memory and looking up information in the world depending on access cost (as summarised by Maglio et al. 2003).
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a cost-sensitive probe policy rather than always probing.

source: Maglio, Wenger & Copeland (2003) cost estimate is conservative
finding: Authors note their cost estimate (two keypresses) overstates the cost for real experts, who have internalised the strategy. So the real benefit-to-cost ratio is probably higher than reported.
numbers: Cost = twice mean keypress RT added to a 4.4 s fixed trial time.
limits: Direction of bias is the authors' claim, untested.
agent_relevance: Probe costs should be measured per agent and task, not assumed.

source: Maglio & Wenger (2000) mechanism background: physical rotation can help or hurt mental rotation
finding: Notes that physically rotating objects can help or hurt mental rotation depending on conditions, so physical rotation may do more than substitute for mental rotation. Kirsh and Maglio themselves speculated it cues retrieval.
numbers: No numbers; cites Wexler and colleagues (1997, 1998) and Wohlschlager and Wohlschlager (1998).
limits: Secondhand citations only.
agent_relevance: The mechanism is debated (substitution, priming, cueing). Each implies a different design for LLM probes.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 as bandit agents with history in the prompt. Only one setup explored properly: GPT-4 with chain of thought and an externally summarised history given as sufficient statistics. All others failed to explore.
numbers: Basic GPT-4 prompt showed suffix failures (never picks the best arm after some round) in over 60% of replicates. Failure modes: suffix failure and near-uniform play across arms.
limits: Small bandit tasks. Authors say external summarisation may not be possible in complex settings, and suggest fine-tuning may be needed.
agent_relevance: Models do not spontaneously probe well. Probing needs structure in the scaffold (summaries, explicit statistics).

source: Li, Kim & Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information?
finding: Models do well at choosing the clarifying question on math tasks but poorly on logic and planning tasks. Being able to solve the fully specified problem was not enough to ask the right question.
numbers: Subset check: 99.39% on GSME-Q and 84.05% on GSM-Q, but only 40 to 50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q (abstract). Accuracy falls with number of variables, constraints and search depth (Spearman correlations mostly negative).
limits: One missing variable only; multiple-choice question selection, not free asking. Table cells in the text extraction are partly scrambled, so the cell-to-model mapping was not checked.
agent_relevance: Knowing what to probe is the hard step, not doing the probe. The schema should name the unknown first and rank candidate probes.

source: Kobalczyk & van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Choosing clarifying questions by expected information gain over sampled candidate solutions gave higher accuracy with fewer queries than letting the model pick questions by reasoning alone.
numbers: Coding test: 4 elicited requirements, 20 sampled solutions per step, averaged over 48 tasks, 3 run and 3 evaluation seeds, four models (Llama3-8B, Llama3-70B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini). Gap between EIG and baseline smaller for stronger models. Exact accuracies only in appendix tables, not extracted.
limits: Answers come from simulated users or test cases. Gain shrinks as the model gets stronger.
agent_relevance: Sample candidate hypotheses, then pick the probe that best splits them: a usable probe-selection rule.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Running the code and feeding back execution results improves generated code. Gains up to 12% with unit tests, and 2 to 3% on Spider (9% on the hardest problems) with code explanation only.
numbers: MBPP baseline vs with execution trace feedback (no unit tests): Codex 61.4 to 66.2, GPT-3.5 67.6 to 69.2, GPT-4 72.8 to 76.4. Over 12% on TransCoder and 8% on MBPP for GPT-4 with unit tests. Spider: greedy plus debugging matched the 16-sample baseline; 8 samples plus debugging beat 32 samples. One debug turn usually enough (later turns within 0.1%).
limits: Without unit test execution GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were overconfident and gained little (up to about 1%, 3.6% on MBPP for GPT-4). GPT-3.5 on TransCoder stayed at 89.1 in every row.
agent_relevance: Execution is the real probe. Without a world to run it in, self-explanation helps much less; the information comes from the run.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Repairing code after a failed run often gives little over sampling more programs at the same compute. The bottleneck is the model's own diagnosis of what went wrong. Better feedback gives larger gains.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 samples then 1 repair each (up to 20 total) gives 1.05x the pass@20 rate; 2 samples then 10 repairs each (22 total) gives 0.97x. Repair success with GPT-4's own feedback 33.30% (introductory 42.64, interview 19.33, competition 3.67) vs human feedback 52.60% (62.21, 45.67, 14.67), 1.58x. 16 human participants.
limits: Python function tasks (HumanEval, APPS); small human study. Results vary a lot across subsets and some conditions show no benefit.
agent_relevance: A probe only helps if its result is interpreted well. Spend budget on diverse first attempts plus good diagnosis, not many blind repairs.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting
finding: Interleaving actions (look something up, take a step) with reasoning beat acting without thoughts on interactive tasks. This is probe-then-think in a loop.
numbers: ALFWorld: best ReAct 71% vs best Act 45% vs BUTLER 37%; even the worst ReAct trial (48%) beat both. Relative gain over Act 33% to 90%, mean 62% over six trials. WebShop: +10% absolute over previous best. Fever: ReAct 60.9 vs CoT 56.3.
limits: Few-shot prompting on a small set of environments. The actions are mostly information retrieval, not tested as pure epistemic actions. Acting without thoughts lost track of state.
agent_relevance: Acting and thinking together beat acting alone; action without reasoning fails to decompose goals.

source: Gap note: no LLM test of Kirsh and Maglio's hypothesis by name found
finding: No study was found that tests the Kirsh and Maglio epistemic-action hypothesis on a language model by name. The nearest evidence is on execution feedback, clarifying questions and exploration. The search budget ran out before a systematic sweep.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Absence is not shown, only not found. arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate limited; web search was exhausted after the first query.
agent_relevance: Treat the link from human epistemic action to LLM probing as an analogy backed by indirect evidence.
